utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume with the Judges present as we indicated, in full agreement. Let me make sure everybody can hear me first. Mr. Harmon, do you hear me, all though I know you understand French. I would like to say good afternoon to everybody, first the interpreters. I hope that the weekend has been good and let me remind you that we are meeting pursuant to Rule 71, acting as presiding officers in order to allow the hearings to continue in the absence of Judge Riad for exceptional circumstances. Since the Judge is not in the Netherlands at moment. Let me remind you for the transcript that this was done in full agreement. Please be seated (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: With the Defence and the Prosecution. Also let me remind you that we will finish with our hearings on Thursday afternoon, not on Friday, and we will try to sit on Wednesday morning, let me turn to the legal officer. I think there is an initial appearance, but I don't think that will prevent us from doing it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we begin -- can we start the initial hearing at 9.30? I am going to turn to Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, then we would start at 9.30. This actually involves another Trial Chamber. Judge Rodriguez would probably have no problems with that either, which would mean that this Blaskic trial would start a bit later. Let me turn to the witness, say good afternoon to him, I hope that he has had a good weekend. And let me remind him that he is still under oath in front of only two Judges. It might be surprising to him but I believe the Defence counsel must have explained to him why we are acting as we are, but changes nothing respect of himself, except that he will not hear Judge Riad asking any questions, but Judge Riad gave to us the questions that he wanted to ask, possibly. And if he has other questions, he can read the transcript and then ask the questions further to that. Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. As the Court recalls, it addressed a comment to the witness at the end of the session last week and the witness expressed concern to me whether he could respond, there was something he wanted to say. I told him if the Court would allow, that I could summarise his response perhaps briefly for the Court. And that is to say that he understands that his cross-examination testimony is different in a qualitative sense from his direct examination testimony, and he simply wanted to state that on direct examination he had a chance to review all of the documents in advance. The documents he was shown had been preselected as documents that he recalled, or could authenticate through personal knowledge. On cross-examination, he has not seen documents before in terms of preparing for his testimony, some he has never seen before, and others he has not seen for five years. So, he simply wishes to state to the court through me or directly, that if he appears to be hesitating or taking his time to look at these documents on cross-examination, it is a different procedure from what was used to prepare his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I know how talented you are when it comes to defending General Blaskic and I see that you are acting with as much assiduity for the defence of your witness. But he was not being attacked, I want you to understand that, he was not being attacked. I simply wanted to say, and that is my duty to say it, if necessary, and I will then give the witness the floor, in this Tribunal the Judges have an absolute and essential necessity that is to reach the truth which, of course, is also in the interest of the accused first and foremost. Such a long testimony and such a compact and full testimony by necessity can be valued only in respect of its general cohesiveness. And that was the only message that I had allowed myself, personally, in fact what I said only engages myself. But I am profoundly engaged by what I said. If one looks at the Rules and the Statute, one sees that the Judges have a great deal of power allowing them to attempt to reach the truth in a case and one of those powers, in fact, is to order the witnesses who are under oath to be careful that there be a degree of cohesiveness in everything that is being said. Would you like to add something to that, Brigadier? You are absolutely free to add something if you wish to do so, especially in light of what I just said and what Mr. Hayman said. Speak freely, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good day. In relation to what Mr. Hayman has said, and in relation to your suggestion, I have nothing special to add. May I just say that what I shall be saying will be possibly as clear as possible, but when I cannot directly explain things, I shall kindly ask you to bear with me and I'm not going to prejudge anything. I am sure that every question will be responded to adequately, but I shall certainly act on your advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, I think I can speak on behalf of Judge Shahabuddeen to thank you for those clarifications. We can now resume our work and, Mr. Kehoe, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, counsel, good afternoon Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn our attention initially --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn our attention initially to the Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/6, Defence Exhibit 405 and then Prosecution Exhibit 456/7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Usher, the Defence Exhibit chronologically comes between the two, 456/6 and 456/7. I will show you the ones in the series. The 16th goes first, this goes second and chronologically that goes third, great. Thank you. Mr. Dubuisson, while we're talking about these exhibits, with your permission, if you could pull out the photograph 80/7, Prosecutor's 80/7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, just going back to the order of Blaskic that we had introduced, talked about on Friday, 456/6, is the order of the 16th of January 1993, which orders, among other things, to take shifts off the line against the Chetniks in full readiness for action against the Muslim forces, and on number 5, calls upon the 4th Military Battalion to control traffic, confiscate equipment and weapons from all Muslim transports. Now, shortly after that you talked during your direct examination with Mr. Nobilo about 405, Defence Exhibit 405, which is an order of 21 January 1993; do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was written by you, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it, and it was signed by Franjo Nakic, Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is upon the order of the chief of the main staff in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen from the preamble of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without reading the whole thing the order basically notes that the units in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone should establish contact with competent command of the BH army in your zone of responsibility and settle all controversial issues by means of agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says in this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is signed by Franjo Nakic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as authorised by General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to the 23rd of January 1993, Exhibit 456/7, and that order is signed by Colonel Blaskic himself, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the signature of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's read this. This is the 23rd of January 1993, approximately two days after this order of the 21st of January, saying "settle controversial issues with the Bosnia government." It says on the 23rd of January 1993, and it is essentially to all of the commands in Central Bosnia, and we will read it. "Due to the need to newly arisen needs and intensified enemy activities of our former allies, who formed in three member groups called Troika, attack our units, crews, manning weapons and individuals, I hereby issue the following order: 1. HVO personnel shall raise their alertness and tighten their personal security measures in keeping with their duties in HVO units. 2. The command post and HVO personnel in the field or on leave shall be constantly under increased security. 3. This order shall be carried out immediately and commanders of brigades and independent units of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command shall be responsible to me for its execution." Signed by Colonel Blaskic, 23 January 1993. Now, on the 23rd of January 1993, Blaskic has ordered HVO troops onto a heightened security level, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is not what it says in this order. Mr. President, Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to go back to the document of January 10th, 1993, because on Friday when we had a discussion here, I said that I cannot exactly recall the circumstances under which it was created. Over the weekend I thought about this document and the exact time when this document was made in the main headquarters and when it came to the Operative Zone and on the basis of that document, we gave these orders 456/6. The reason for making such a document is that there was a conflict between the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf. Gornji Vakuf as a municipality is a neighbouring municipality to the municipality of Novi Travnik which was under the command of the Operational Zone, because of that conflict and because of its intensity, the head of the main staff of the HVO issued orders to the commander of the Zone of Central Bosnia to take those measures which the commander did give in his orders. Why traffic control and why observation of traffic communications? Gornji Vakuf was under the zone of command of the 3rd Corps, the 3rd Corps with its command posts in Zenica sent orders to Gornji Vakuf and sent reinforcements to the units that were fighting in that town and also sent materiel and technical support with a view to helping them. It is only natural that in a situation of war the HVO functioned as an entity and the head of the main staff would issue orders for traffic control so that you would monitor all communication lines. That is why this order was created. Not for the reasons that the Prosecutor seems to be indicating in his questions. This can be checked whether at that time there was a conflict in Gornji Vakuf or not, but there are facts and documents supporting this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, the HVO in various locales, Gornji Vakuf and Vitez did, in fact, operate as an entity, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not cooperate with Gornji Vakuf in the sense of us communicating with them directly. I mean, the Operative Zone and them. But we got orders from the head of the main staff and who commanded both Gornji Vakuf and Central Bosnia, so he was in command of the entire HVO. And he gave orders to the commander of the Operative Zone to undertake these measures. It is only according to military logic and any other action --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, the question and what you said in testimony is, "it is only natural in a situation of war the HVO function was an entity and the head of the main staff would issue orders for traffic control that you would monitor all communication lines." And my question is: Based on what you said, it's true, is it not, that the HVO operated as an entire entity, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO under the command of the main staff and on the basis of orders of the main staff, they acted in accordance with the orders of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in these orders, 456/6 and 456/7, the HVO is on heightened security; correct, on both of the orders and documents that Blaskic gives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but it can be seen quite clearly what activities are being taken. There is no move of forces, there are no orders to attack. Only to observe the area, only to observe the communication lines and if the 3rd Corps were to move along communication lines, that is to say if materiel and technical support were to be given to Gornji Vakuf, that that should be stopped and this should be taken away from them. It is only logical in a situation of war, but there is no move of forces there and no orders to attack any unit of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's look at Defence Exhibit 407, and if we could put Prosecution Exhibit 8/7, the photograph, on the ELMO, and if the Brigadier could look at this Defence exhibit, as well. 407, Mr. President, is a document from the 27th of January 1993 signed by Franjo Nakic, but written by the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, you note in this document that you wrote, Defence Exhibit 407, that in the afternoon hours of the 24th of January, 1993, Muslim forces erected a barricade at a previously prepared location in Kacuni near Busovaca, and it goes onto say they stopped five UN vehicles. Now, you previously identified an individual in 80/7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you put that back on there, please, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man you identified as Ignac Kostromann is on the left, is he not? Can you point to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Mr. Kostromann.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the events that you described in your report, Kostromann was stopped and arrested by Muslim forces in around, between Kacuni and Bijelovats at a checkpoint; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and we got that in the report from the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not in your report, that fact is not in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When it happened, that is to say, when Mr. Kostromann was stopped and taken prisoner and the commander of the Operative Zone sent a report to that effect. If we informed someone else of this too, it is only natural because we received it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, nevertheless, Blaskic was supposed to be heading in the same direction as Kostromann at the time that Kostromann was arrested, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that day whether Blaskic was supposed to take the same route at the same time as Mr. Kostromann did, but I know that if General Blaskic was supposed to go to Kiseljak, the only way is through Kacuni, or rather, by the place where the checkpoint was, and whether the checkpoint was there or not, and at what time, that is what I cannot tell at this stage without having a document, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, isn't it true that the arrest of Mr. Kostromann by this checkpoint greatly angered not only Mr. Kostromann but Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it angered Mr. Kostromann I don't know, because Mr. Kostromann was not a member of the command of the Operative Zone, so it's not that I could have discussed it with him. How angry General Blaskic was, I cannot say for sure either, but it is certain that, as far as I know, it seems to me that Mr. Kostromann was secretary of the HDZ. He was involved in politics. I wasn't involved in politics. It is certain that this was an unfortunate incident, primarily because this is, this was an official of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims let him go, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember the report Mr. Kostromann was released, and what happened at that point when he was stopped without a report from the Brigade Nikola Subic-Zrinski, I could not say exactly now. But according to the information I have, he was taken out of his vehicle, he was made to stand there at gun point with a pistol pointed at him, and I know perhaps the Defence could help me with this document, because I know they have this document, the report of the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade, and then I can tell you exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't have the document, Judge, maybe the Defence has it and wants to help the Court, the prosecutor, and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have anything here now. Whether we have it or not, we do not intend to assist the Prosecutor. It is not customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I didn't ask for the assistance, the witness did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's the witness who asked it. It was your witness who asked for it. It was the Brigadier who asked for the document. It wasn't Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is D407 so, if possible, this report can be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no, no, it wasn't that. But we shouldn't continue with this incident. I think it simply is a rectification I wanted to make, and it was your own witness who said there must and document which told about the kidnapping of Mr. Kostromann. If you don't have it, you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, I do not remember this event. For me personally it was not an important incident, but, at this point, I cannot say whether the Defence has it or not because I cannot recall the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, just continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, after the release of Kostromann, didn't Blaskic send units from Busovaca down to this checkpoint on the same day to try to break through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony is you don't know anything about that incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said what I know about the incident. I know that he was stopped. I know that he was retained at the checkpoint. And what happened after that, I mean, I know that he was released, too, that is a fact. The other details I cannot retell now, because I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what do you recall, sir? What details do you recall, what happened after Kostromann was released? What response did the HVO have to the arrest of Ignac Kostromann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall say what I recall, and what was in the report of the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade. A report arrived stating that Mr. Kostromann had been stopped, mistreated at that checkpoint, mistreated, and then released. I would appreciate it if you could tell me the date when this occurred, because I cannot remember the date now when this happened to Kostromann.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you were there, your report was of the 27th of January 1993, and it relates to facts that started on the 24th of January 1993. So, you have to tell me and the Court when this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the report the Prosecutor is drawing my attention to, again, analyses the events of the 24th, the 25th and the 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, the incident concerning Ignac Kostromann, let me withdraw that question. This particular report deals with the Busovaca area; does it not? The left hand corner it says "Busovaca area situation report," right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing in this report discusses the events concerning the arrest of Ignac Kostromann, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This event, the arrest of Ignac Kostromann is not mentioned specifically because it says here on the date of the 24th, such and such a thing happened and on the 25th such and such a thing happened and on the 26th such and such a thing happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, based on that report, the events that took place, the fighting started on the 24th of January 1993, according to the report that you have in your hands; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What it exactly says here is the following: "On the 24th of January 1993 in the afternoon hours, the Muslim forces erected barricades at a previously prepared location in Kacuni near Busovaca. They stopped five UN vehicles, tanks and a regular military police patrol vehicle, fired a hand-held rocket launcher and opened intensive small arms fire which wounded HVO military police deputy commander in Busovaca, Mr. Ivo Perovic. After a brutal torture his throat was cut and his body was delivered to the HVO on the 25th of January 1993 at 1 hours. A taxi driver who was there by chance ran to help the wounded Ivo, but he was hit by a contact rifle grenade at close range." That is what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact of the matter that is, that nothing about Kostromann is in that report; correct? And you said, according to that report, the fighting started on the 24th; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the paragraph I read out does not speak about the beginning of fighting, but it speaks of an incident that happened at a checkpoint and where a man lost his life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like us to move forward. It's a very simple question. Does the report deal with this arrest of Mr. Kostromann, "yes" or "no"? Mr. Kehoe, be very clear when you ask your questions. The question is clear. You're the one who wrote the report, I imagine, theoretically, as I can see it here, this does not deal with Mr. Kostromann's arrest. Perhaps you were thinking about it, perhaps he is alluding to it indirectly and you're referring to other documents, only you can know. Please answer the Prosecutor's question, the question that he asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this report does not deal with the incident of Mr. Kostromann's arrest, because it can be seen from the text itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the 24th you told us that Blaskic was down in Kiseljak throughout the entire conflict in late January and early February 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic, that is correct, was in Kiseljak throughout the conflict. The exact date when he went there, that I cannot tell, but I do know that he went before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 509A, A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, document 509 emanates from the command of the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak on 20 January 1993 signed by Mijo Bozic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this is Mijo's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want to compare it to one of the Defence documents that you previously identified as Mijo Bozic? Because if you want to do that, we can look at Defence Exhibit 200, which you identified as Mijo Bozic's signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no need for that. I do remember, it's a bit illegible here, but I remember the way Mijo used to sign his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, in fact, Mijo Bozic's signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so as of the 20th of January 1993, would you agree with me that Mijo Bozic is now the brigade commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this point I cannot remember when Mijo became commander, whether it was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's read the order and see if the context of this particular order clarifies things for you. And it's an order from the command of the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, number 01117 January 1993, the date is 20 January 1993. "For the purpose of the complete engagement of the brigades military intelligence service and the establishment and organisation of these services in the battalions, I hereby issue the following order: For all Voss officers in the battalions to submit comprehensive biographies and the evaluations of the battalion commanders and the SIS, Information and Security Service, officers concerning the proposed personnel. 2. The biographies and evaluations shall be submit to the brigade's Voss organ, at the latest, by 1700 hours on 22 January 1993. 3. The battalion commanders and the SIS officials of the battalions are responsible to me for the execution of this order. CC commanders of the battalions 1 through 3", the balance of that is illegible and it is signed "commander" with the signature of Mijo Bozic; is that right, sir? It would appear that as of the 20th of January 1993, Mijo Bozic, who was in Blaskic's headquarters in Vitez, had been transferred to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we're talking about this transfer I know this happened in January, but I don't know the exact date, and that Mijo was appointed to that duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in any event, at that particular time, or excuse me, after the 24th, 25th of January 1993, Blaskic himself is down in Kiseljak, and he was located in Kiseljak in the Kiseljak barracks, which is where the Ban Jelacic Brigade was; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic, at the time of the conflict in Busovaca in January was in Kiseljak, and he was located, that is communications with us were done through the command of the brigade in Kiseljak, and he therefore used the links and communications that that brigade had at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the brigade was garrisoned and stationed at the Kiseljak barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was, yes. Its command was in one of the facilities of the barracks in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you another document, sir. Mr. President, I have a rough translation of this in English. It is in BCS. I'll gladly read the rough translation and should anybody feel that that translation is incorrect, certainly I'm sure we will all discuss it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 510, it's only in BCS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, take a look at this document, 510, is that Mijo Bozic's signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is Mijo Bozic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let me read this from the rough translation and you correct me if there is anything wrong here. "27 January 1993, order on offensive military action..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't read too fast, Mr. Kehoe, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "27 January, 1993, order on offensive military action, to the commander of the 1st Battalion. Due to the negative developments in the theatre of operations and the impossibility to take the villages of Bukovci due to strong lateral fire and the probable participation of the villages of Radeljevici, Pobrdje, Markovici and Maslinovici in a defensive effort I hereby order: 1. That the first company of the 1st Battalion be mobilised immediately and reinforced with anti-commando platoons and transported by armoured personnel carrier to the village of Datici, Datici formed up and that upon making preparations for opening fire, disarm the villages of Radeljevici, Pobrdje, Markovici and Maslinovici. Readiness at point of departure, 1600 hours. Readiness for opening mortar fire," time is illegible, but it looks in the original to be 1300 or 1800, I'm not sure. "Preparations for opening fire to be carried out from 1600 to 1630, with ten shells each for 82 millimetre and 122 millimetre mortar and targets in villages selected. Upon completing preparations, demand that the local population unconditionally surrender all their armaments as otherwise the village will be burned to the ground. In case of refusal to surrender weapons, open strong and concentrated fire from all targets from anti-aircraft guns, anti-aircraft machine guns and mortars and proceed with mopping up operations. 3. After taking the villages, pursue the enemy towards the village of Bukovci with a view towards destroying that village and breaking up the enemy forces in it. We will have to be able to take the village of Bukovci by night fall on the condition that we torch everything we find in our path. I appoint Mato Lucic brigade commander, co-ordinator of this action and Marinko Tuka his deputy. Inform me regularly every two hours of all important events and extraordinary ones." The rest is illegible. "6. That operations start at" illegible "signal" and the CC is "the 1st Battalion commander and the 2nd Artillery commander" and signed by commander Mijo Bozic: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you a map, sir, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 511.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For reference purposes, Mr. President, this is a smaller version of Exhibit 29, which is the large one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I show you this map, which has been identified as Exhibit 511, and you can see the villages in and around the Kiseljak area that are mentioned in this order. Do you see them highlighted in yellow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see them highlighted in that manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can see that the initial meeting point and the goal being going towards Bukovci, which is in between Bijelovats and Kacuni; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but Bukovci is nearest to the village of Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Now, Brigadier, those are predominantly Muslim villages, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether they are Muslim villages, because I never lived in the Kiseljak municipality area. But I would like to say something with regard to the order as a soldier and the conditions governing that order, although I didn't see the order and I'm not familiar with the text of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sure -- I promise you can say what you want to say, but try to answer the questions and afterwards make some comments. You can make your comments, but first answer the question directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, based on paragraph two, completing preparations, "Demand the local population unconditional surrender, all their armaments, as otherwise the villages will be burned to the ground." This is an order given by a HVO brigade commander. Do you conclude as a military officer and a military man that those villages were Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now answer the Prosecutor's questions and then you can make any additional comments you like about the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, judge, I'm not getting translation. INTERPRETER: Repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please repeat, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that the order was given as it stands, and because they were Muslim villages, because I don't know whether the villages were exclusively populated by the Muslims. As I said, the national structure of these villages is not known to me. The document that we're talking about, that we're discussing, that is to say this order which was issued in the Ban Jelacic Brigade, came into being under conditions when the war in the area of the Busovaca municipality and the Kiseljak municipality, that is to say they were intensified operations, and when the whole area of Kacuni, Bijelovats and the other settlements between Kiseljak and Busovaca were placed under the control of the BH army. This kind of order, if it was given at this particular place, had as its goal to stop those attacks, that is to say to stop the attacks and to prevent a further escalation of the control of the corridor between Kacuni and Kiseljak in the area where these conflicts took place. Now, as far as those events and this document, I don't know the circumstances in which they came into being. That is what I can say as a soldier and officer in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you would agree with me that this order in both paragraph 2 and paragraph 3 gives orders to a battalion that was commanded by Mato Lucic to burn villages to the ground if they are not disarmed, and then after, on paragraph 3, after taking the villages and pursuing the enemy to Bukovci, with a view to destroying that village and breaking up the enemy forces, then it says: "By night fall, take Bukovci by night fall on the condition we torch everything we find in our path." Now, this particular order, sir, is an order by a brigade commander, Mijo Bozic, to burn houses, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned colleague said that the translation is not an authorised one, and therefore, I can conclude from the question that the finesses of the translation are not quite clear. And in point 2, as far as I understand it, and it is my mother tongue, it is stated that the population be threatened, that their village will be burned down if they do not give their arms. It is not an order to burn the villages. It is an order to threaten the population, that unless they lay down their arms their village will be burned. That is to say, if the population do not surrender their arms, and then the second sentence states what is going to be done, and it does not say to burn the village in sentence to point 2, should they fail to surrender their arms, a strong fire should be opened, et cetera, et cetera. So, point 2, which is the crucial point in sentence one, it is stated the type of threat that should be made, regardless of the fact that you can condemn a threat of that kind. And point 2, second sentence says what should be done if they fail to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo, it was very helpful. Of course, it is your native language, but it is important enough that in agreement with Judge Shahabuddeen we would ask the interpreters to reread the entire paragraph 2 and 3 and read them slowly. I think that would be the best thing to do. I will ask the interpreters, or am asking the interpreters to read us paragraphs 2 and 3. Mr. Dubuisson suggests that the witness should read paragraphs 2 and 3, slowly, and the interpreters, who work for the Tribunal have taken oaths of their own, will make a very faithful translations of those paragraphs. And I thank you Mr. Nobilo having raised this very significant question, it is important in respect of your accused, but it is also important for the Prosecution. Therefore, Brigadier, if you agree to go back to paragraphs 2 and 3, read them slowly and the interpreters will do the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, point 2, paragraph 2: "Upon completion of the preparations, to demand of the local population unconditionally to surrender all weapons. If they fail do so, the village will be burned completely. Should they not surrender, reject surrendering their arms, fire will be opened and concentric fire on all goals from PAT and PAM anti-aircraft guns and mortars and a mopping up of the terrain will be undertaken. 3. Upon taking control of these villages, to undertake the, driving out the enemy so that the village of Bukovci could be broken up and destroyed and the enemy forces therein. The village of Bukovci must be taken control of by night fall on condition that we burn everything that is in our path, that stands in our way."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, based on what you just said, on paragraph 2, this is an order that if the villages do not turn over their arms, that their village is going to be burned to the ground; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, in my consultation with Mr. Hayman I maintain that the interpretation is not the correct one, because from one, there is one sentence has been turned into two sentences and I'm talking about the first sentence in point 2, and when you have two sentences, the senses change. We're dealing with one sentence where it states that they be asked to surrender their arms. And that should they fail to do so, the village will be destroyed. So, it is one sentence and not two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we will not have the passages reread. We simply ask the Prosecutor to have the document officially translated by the translation service into English and into French. And if, in light of those translations the Defence has something else to add, it can provide its own translation. Sometimes there are differences in translations, that can happen. The translation must be prepared by tomorrow, and if necessary, the Defence can make its own translation. But this is a very important point, everybody realises this. Yes or no was an order given to burn or was it ordered conditionally, or was it simply a threat? I think this is an important point. Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, turning your attention to number 3, it is clear, is it not, that Mijo Bozic is telling Mato Lucic and his battalion that they must take Bukovci by night fall on the condition that we torch everything that is in our path or in our way? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you agree with that, you have no comment about paragraph 3. I myself heard the translators or the interpreters say under conditions of -- how was it? Under the condition...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think the translator first said, "on the condition that we torch everything that we find in our path," and then there was a translation "on the condition that we find anything in our way."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Brigadier, there is no problem with the translation here in paragraph 2, you have no problem with that, do you, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It has been translated literally, what it says here. But I don't know whether in the English language it has the same meaning. In the Croatian language, that which is found in one's path is an obstacle, it is something that impedes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo's speech, let the translators translate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, if this continues we are going to recruit you as a translator for the International Criminal Tribunal. Let's state that point for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I object to counsel interrupting my learned colleague, but I would like to say, and I think Judge Shahabuddeen, who speaks my language, is in a good position to see that the translation in English doesn't make sense. "We must take Bukovci by night fall on the condition that we torch everything that is in our path." It doesn't make sense in the English language. There has to be some meaning full translation of the phrase, and I think had we will get there, and by what process I'm not sure, but I don't know, Mr. President, if you're getting the same strange translation that us English speakers are getting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman, I will admit that in French when one says under the condition that especially under the condition can be interpreted in various ways. We will ask the chief of the translation service to give us a translation of this text in English and in French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, the goal of this particular battalion was to take Bukovci; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you didn't ask a question. This is a very simple question that the witness was asked. You don't have to intervene unless you want to talk about the translation. But we're now talking about paragraph 3 where it says that there was an order to take Bukovci. That is the question that the witness is being asked. You are not being asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Mr. President, but we have ascertained that as far as two essential points are concerned, we cannot use this document, and the document is an organic hole, so I suggest that questions in relation to this document be put once a complete translation is provided, otherwise a mistake can be made. That the only thing I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Agree with Mr. Nobilo, I would like this document to be translated by this evening into French and English and tomorrow we will take up this conversation again, that is, the discussion about document 510. All right, Mr. Kehoe, please move to another document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning our attention, Brigadier, to the actual map, 511, and the individual villages that are highlighted on it, were those villages burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether those villages were burned or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, without going into the content of this document, Judge, I'm not going to go in there, talking about those paragraphs, but you will agree with me, Brigadier, that this Mijo Bozic order was dated the 27th of January and they were due to begin to execute this at 1600 hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see the document now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, give that document back to him, document 510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Was the attack ordered for the 27th of January? For the date I think there is no translation problem, don't you agree, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this document, I don't see the exact date. I see a signal and I can't read it, that operation should be started on signal, and I don't see anything after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, up in the upper left-hand corner the date is 27 January 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we already said we would talk about this document tomorrow. I don't want you to ask many more questions, but if you have a question about the date and the time, he can say that, he can answer or not answer. He can answer this question immediately and then we will move to another question. All right, was the order of the attack, according to this that you read in your own language, that it was the 27th of January 1993, that's the only part in Serbo-Croat that I myself can translate, but I don't know whether it was 4:00 in the afternoon or not. If you don't want to answer, then we will go back to this question tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second half of paragraph 1 it says readiness, that's the start position at 1600 hours. 1600 hours is what is stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Turn your attention to Defence Exhibit 348. Now, Brigadier, the particular document we just looked at, the order, had an execution date of 1600 hours. Now, before you is Defence Exhibit 348, which is a cease-fire agreement signed by Colonel Blaskic at 1740 hours; do you see that? Upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: On top of the document at the top of the document. You're used to reading orders, I'm sure you can find the time. At the top, it says 1745. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is dated this, particular order, this Defence Exhibit 348 is dated the same day as the Mijo Bozic attack order; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the order of Mijo Bozic was written on the 27th and this document was also written on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this, sir, was written approximately an hour and 40 minutes after the attack was supposed to begin; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turn to paragraph 1, paragraph one states that this goes into effect at midnight on the 28th of January 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the previous document noted that Bozic ordered Lujic to take those villages, or take Bukovci by night fall; didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blaskic issue an order to stop the attacks on this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether an order was issued, but this order which I have before me was given on the basis of an agreement, the time when the agreement came into force, that is, it is the 28th of January 1993 at 1.00. And that was probably an agreement reached, and this order on the cessation of hostilities is the result of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, on the 27th of January, based on your direct testimony, Blaskic is in Kiseljak, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he signs this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he sign this is cease-fire agreement at 1740 on the 27th to take effect at midnight on the 28th; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the agreement was signed, actually signed, I don't know. But I do know that it comes into force on the 28th of January 1993, which can be seen from the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit 511, the map we just talked about, right over to your left. Did Blaskic stop the shelling of these villages on the 27th, or did he go ahead with it and allow them to go ahead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not know whether the shelling was stopped. And I don't know whether the shelling actually took place or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we will move on to another subject, and we will come back after a full translation. Mr. President, with the Court's permission I would like to ask a few more questions concerning Exhibit 510, the order that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Let me call your attention to the fact that the deadline for execution was the 28th of January, 1:00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right, midnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 28 January at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I wanted to ask this question: The implication in your questions is that this order of the 27th of January 1993 should have operated to inhibit the execution of the order in Prosecutor's Exhibit 510.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But if you exclude the manner of implementing the order in Exhibit 510, was there anything in the new order which prohibited the implementation from the previous order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Judge, except, of course, that the previous order, we can discuss this with the translation, if it calls upon the burning of houses, is an illegal order. But as far as the actual attack goes, no, but it goes, I believe, Judge, to the spirit of an actual cease-fire agreement which is trying to be implemented. And we have an order to take these villages by midnight, and then a cease-fire agreement that comes in effect at 12.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your questions are directed to the spirit of the thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want to thank Judge Shahabuddeen, which again gives me the occasion to ask you, Mr. Kehoe, to get to your comments and observations more directly. Let's not keep turning around and around all kinds of questions in order to get to what you're going at. You're trying to get something, go there directly and we will make our evaluation thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to another subject concerning the conflict in January and February and I want you to look at Defence Exhibit 409 of the 29th of January 1993. Now, Brigadier, this is a document that was signed by Franjo Nakic on the 29th of January 1993 at 2020 hours. I just want to go to the first paragraph here that starts "In the course..." "In the course of today the lines of defence have remained unchanged. A 45 kilometre long front has been established. Our defence is positioned and well entrenched, further entrenchments are being completed, a fire system has been organised and the situation is under control." Do you see that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sentence that starts: "Our defence is positioned and well entrenched, further entrenchments are being completed." We are talking there about the digging of trenches in this particular document, are we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this document, or rather in this paragraph, mention is made of the situation at the front-line, not about digging trenches, so the situation has not been changed during the course of that day. That is to say, that a cease-fire had entered into force, operations had stopped; however, the troops remained in trenches, because it is only these further measures that should be taken that are going to separate the two armies. However, nothing was done, and the two armies remained at that front-line until the Washington Accords were signed. So, now they are talking about the situation as it is on the ground. On one hand is the army of the BH and on the other side is the HVO and that is what this report refers to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a simple question, Brigadier. When Nakic says "further entrenchments are being completed," he is talking about trenches being dug at the front-line, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is important to note here, Mr. President, is that further entrenchments are being completed, not simply entrenchments. So, that is to say that if a soldier started digging a dug out on one day, and then for several days after that he --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we're talking about is the continued digging of trenches, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel should not interrupt the witness. If the court perceives a problem, the Court can interrupt the witness. That is not a power within counsel's proper authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is a very simple question as to whether further entrenchments means to continue the digging of trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Hayman pointed out that you interrupted the witness. Try to let the witness speak. The day that Mr. Hayman will interrupt the witness, I will point that out to him, as well, but for the time you're the one who interrupted the witness. Let the witness make his explanations, but I ask him to be specific in his answers to go as quickly as he can to the point that he is trying to get at. Go ahead, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, further entrenchments, as far as I understand military terminology, and as far as I remember the situation on the ground, meant in this situation to repair that which has already been done. Because the army, the troops, had to be there on the front-line, and not that level of agreement had been reached which would completely separate the two armies, so the people were there and they continued to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, did you go to the front-line to observe the digging of trenches at the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I did not go to the front-line to watch trench digging because I had things to do at the command of the Operative Zone. And during the fighting I never had an opportunity to go to the front-line, because as the head of operations, I had to collect information and work at the operational centre. Mr. President, with your permission, we shall move on to the next sentence and we are going to understand it. "During the day the enemy violated the signed cease-fire several times," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like things to be very clear. The questions must be asked clearly and then answered. Brigadier, have you to answer the question and then we move on to another one. Otherwise we are not going to find a way out of this. Was your question answered, Mr. Kehoe? And if so, please ask another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will move on to the next question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me direct your attention to 1 February 1993. Was then Colonel Blaskic in the Lasva Valley area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 1st of February 1992, to the best of my knowledge, General Blaskic was not there. Unless some negotiations or meetings were organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm talking about on 1 February 1993 and you answered February 1992, I don't know if that was a slip of the tongue, but my question was, was he in the Vitez area on 1 February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1st of February 1993, to the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you told us during direct examination that he was in the Kiseljak area throughout the entire time of the conflict; is that right? Or is there -- are you somewhat doubtful of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no doubts concerning that. I only could not give a direct answer because perhaps UNPROFOR had organised a meeting on how the cease-fire would be conducted. But in his capacity of commander of the Operational Zone, that he was staying at the Lasva Valley at that particular point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, if he came to Vitez or the Vitez area on the 1st of February 1993, he certainly would come to his headquarters, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic did not stop by the command on the mentioned day, the 1st of February 1993. So, I said that I do not know that he was in the area of the Lasva River Valley. So, I stick to the statement I made, that at that time he was in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard of General Morillon, but I have not met him, so I don't know him personally, but I have heard of him, because of the post he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can take a break now, because we're about to move into another subject here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we have a long afternoon, we're going to take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, ask the appropriate service to be sure that we don't freeze to death in this room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will take care of it immediately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: These are long trials, but if the Judges or the counsel get sick on top of it, it really isn't a good thing. All right, we will now resume, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to read a document which is in English, I hand it out to all parties so everybody can read along. Mr. President, this is a military information summary from the British Battalion, the Cheshire regimen, of 1 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 512.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I realise this is in English, but I would like to read to you, and if we could put it on the ELMO, the second paragraph on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, we are not going to read the entire document, I put the document in its entirety so nothing would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please read slowly so the interpreters can interpret it. They don't have the document, they have to look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1 February, 1993, 1 Cheshire, no info sum number 93, dated 1 February 1993. 1. Vitez. We will skip the first paragraph and move to the second paragraph, the one beginning "General Morillon." That's good. "General Morillon hosted talks between 3rd Corps BiH commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, HVO Central Bosnia, Commander Jusic Kadir, BiH Visoko and EC monitors at Bila school. "Agreement was reached on the withdrawal of external forces from the Busovaca/Kacuni area. All external forces are to be withdrawn from the area by 1300 hours on 2 February 1993. "Discussions also included measures to open all routes, Vitez/Zenica, Kiseljak/Visoko. Work will commence on the main barricade blocking the Vitez to Zenica route at 1400 hours on 2 February, 1993." Now, Brigadier, do you remember this meeting when General Morillon came to the Bila school where the British battalion was garrisoned? Do you remember this meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that a meeting of this kind was held on -- I don't recall the day and time of the meeting, I was not present at the meeting. Everything happened under UNPROFOR organisation, and it was UNPROFOR in charge of all the, the entire organisation, the coming and the going of the participating parties, that was all under UNPROFOR organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time General Morillon was the Commander in Chief of all UNPROFOR forces; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it is. But I cannot say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this particular report indicates that Blaskic was at the Bila school in Stari Bila on 1 February 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this report it can be seen, and I said that the meeting was organised by UNPROFOR, that the participating parties were brought there under the UNPROFOR organisation, and they were returned to their positions, and the places from which they had come to the meeting was also organised by UNPROFOR. That is all I know on the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, how far is the Bila school from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bila school from the Hotel Vitez is about 4 kilometres away, it shouldn't be more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we are talking about an area that is under control of the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area and the venue of the meeting was the UNPROFOR base, and along with the UNPROFOR base on the one hand side were the units of the BiH army and on the other side the HVO units. UNPROFOR was at the Grbavica location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during this period of time Blaskic had ordered meetings to take place to assess what the situation was in his area of control, and this period of time I'm talking about, the first week in February; did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to see a document so that I could know in precise terms what we're talking about and what time we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think there are six copies there, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 513.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. President, there is no French copy of this, so I will have to read the entire page-and-a-half or page-and-three-quarters of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an order of the 4th of February 1993, from the Vitez forward command post, and overcoming the current crisis, order; and it's the attention of commanders of brigades and independent units of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. "On the basis of your reports, the overall situation in units, and in order to overcome the crisis, I hereby order: 1. The assistant commander of SIS shall submit a list of and report on soldiers who have wilfully deserted the line of defence and the reasons for this extraordinary shall be analysed at the command meeting. Officers in charge, brigade commander, assistant for SIS of the Travnik Brigade, dateline 10 February, 1993. 2. The military police commander shall reinforce patrols and guards and shall tighten the security on roads in the area of responsibility of the Travnik Brigade and shall be responsible directly to me for the situation and the measures taken the prisoners under arrest. Officers in charge, assistant for SIS, the commander of the military police, Travnik Brigade, deadline 10 February 1993. 3. Hold meetings, identify persons who have shown negligent and irresponsible conduct or have failed to carry out their tasks, and present evaluation reports for each member of the brigade. Officers in charge commander, deputy commander, dateline 10 February 1993. 4. Carry out the unification of brigades logistics base by unifying the material and redistributing it in sections on two or more locations. Officer in charge, brigade commander, dateline 10 February 1993. 5. Assistant to the commander for SIS shall analyse the security situation and the brigade's area of responsibility with regard to possible sources of the threat to its security, criminals. Officer in charge, assistant to the commander for SIS, deadline 7 February 1993. 6. Immediately have the soldier who sold a rifle to Muslim members of the military police, JF Zenica Brigade, arrested and inform me thereof in writing. Officer in charge, Zenica JF Brigade, military police. Deadline 7 February 1993. 7. Chief of Staff, Franjo Nakic shall supervise the implementation of this order according to deadlines indicated above." And it goes to various units and it's signed someone on behalf of Colonel Blaskic. Whose signature is that on behalf of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the signature of the chief of the main staff, Franjo Nakic, and in the left-hand corner is my own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on number 3, it says that, if you can return to the front page, or you just have a one-page document, but the front page of the English. It says there is an order to hold meetings and identify persons who have known negligent and irresponsible conduct or have failed to carry out their tasks and present evaluation reports for each member of the brigade. The two people he puts, Blaskic puts in charge, is himself and Franjo Nakic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you repeat what you said, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On number 3, the order to hold meetings; does he order himself and Franjo Nakic to conduct those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about holding meetings here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, he gives the responsibility of that to himself and to Franjo Nakic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Holding meetings, these are meetings in the brigade headquarters. And let me clarify the document, if possible, why it was written, how it came about; and that it is not linked to the events we discussed before the break. Because the Travnik Brigade has its defence line towards the army of the Republika Srpska and the problems occurred in that section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question is: Did he hold meetings with the various brigades pursuant to the order that he issued, specifically number 3 in this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meetings were not ordered in the way you describe, but they were ordered, that is to say that the meetings were to be held -- I understand from the text that it was ordered to hold meetings in the brigades themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person responsible for completing this was either Blaskic or Nakic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the responsible individual, that the meetings be held, was the commander of the brigade. The commander of the brigade was to organise the meetings, and he was responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With all due respect, Brigadier, look at number 1 and number 4, the people in charge of those two, and when it is given to the brigade commander, it is listed brigade commander; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I invite you to look at the last eight or ten words in paragraph three, "and present evaluation reports for each member of the brigade"; is it your suggestion that General Blaskic should have done this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, sir, no, sir. I'm merely inquiring, Judge Shahabuddeen, as to whether or not these meetings were conducted by the commander and the deputy commander. I think what it says is present evaluation reports; so, I don't think that he would actually conduct. It says "present evaluation reports for each member of the brigade," so I think the actual evaluation reports that are being presented are either to the commander or the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I'm trying to explore is if there was a plan to have meetings with the brigades to sort out these problems and whether or not Blaskic and Nakic were responsible for being involved in these meetings and completing this task by 10 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Who was responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commanders of the brigades, and all the activities in point 7, from points 1 to point 6, states what should be done, and the control of the implementation will be informed, that they would inform the commander of the main staff. The copy I have is rather illegible, and that is why I find it difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. You would agree with me the person in charge of matters in number 4 is the brigade commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. The brigade commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Careful, Brigadier. When you have a document right in front of you, I'm sure that you recognise this one, you have to try to be logical. When one says commander and deputy commander, what is meant by that. It is in the document the brigade commander. But when Colonel Blaskic means the brigade commander, he says brigade commander; and when he says assistant to the commander, he says it in 5. I want there to be a certain logic in the way you're answering. Do you agree with my comment, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Who was responsible in 3, under 3 who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under 3 it is the commander who is supposed to be responsible. How this word was additionally typewritten, deputy commander, that I really have no idea. I mean, for that large number of brigades, I really have no idea. So, it should be the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The commander is the officer in charge; isn't that right? All right, I have no, I'm not taking sides one or the other, but you are saying it's the brigade commander. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, was Blaskic receiving information from these brigades as to what was happening within their brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic did receive certain information from the brigades. What kind of information was this? When I talked about the system of command, I said that with the brigades we had regular daily communications through daily operative reports that they submitted to us; that is to say, on the situation, the units, the front-lines and other facts that were relevant to each and every brigade. So, that was the most frequent way of informing the commander of the Operational Zone. That is to say, if the commander of the Operational Zone did not give special orders concerning certain events and asking for a special report on certain events. So, regular information was through operative reports, and we had the opportunity of seeing a great many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, Blaskic was receiving information about what was happening with prisoners at the Kaonik camp; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the military prison at Kaonik is concerned, that is what we called it. We did not call it a camp. If you are referring to the prison, the military prison in Kaonik; if you mean a camp in Kaonik, I don't know a camp there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the military prison in Kaonik. Blaskic was getting reports about what was happening in the military prison in Kaonik; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, whether he received them, or whether he received them regularly, or not; but I shall try to remember all the activities concerned and draw a conclusion. The military prison in Kaonik was not in the organisation structure of the command of the Operational Zone. The warden of the military prison in Kaonik was not under the command of General Blaskic, commander of the Operational Zone. Reports, reports on the situation and the way -- and on how people were treated, people who were in the military prison, regardless of whether they were HVO or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did not come regularly. That is to say that the military prison did not send the commander reports every day, what the situation was like, how many prisoners he had, et cetera. If there was some kind of problem where the military was involved, where soldiers were involved, it was to be expected that the warden of the military camp did inform General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn your attention to Defence Exhibit 354. Do you recognise that document, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a document that you identified during the course of your direct testimony, and it is a document that was executed by Blaskic concerning the breaking in to the prison, the Busovaca military prison, by use of arms and the taking of prisoners from their cells. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see it. I remember this document. I remember having identified it when I was answering the questions of the Defence. I do remember this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up in the right-hand corner, up in the upper right-hand corner, what are the two names that are written on there, or the two items that are written in the right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the upper right-hand corner it says in handwriting, Dusko, and it also says prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is Dusko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dusko is Dusko Grubicic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm it on the basis of what it says here; however, guided by logic, when it says to the commander of the HVO Brigade Nikola Subic-Zrinski, one may conclude that he is the person that this is addressed to, but only on the basis of this, where it says Dusko we cannot say for sure that that is the person concerned, Dusko Grubicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was running the military prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The warden of the military prison was in charge of the military prison. I know that it was Zlatko Aleksovski who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I go to private session one moment on this particular document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, private session. All right, then, a closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to this document, Brigadier, 354, it is true that Blaskic was getting information about what was happening inside the Busovaca Military Prison; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said how he could have obtained it, and I cannot confirm that he always received such information. This can best be seen from the top of this document. It probably says on the basis of the report of the responsible persons, et cetera. That is to say, that the warden of the prison was not duty bound to send regular reports to the commander of the operation zone on what was happening in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, is it true that 400 or more Bosnian Muslim prisoners were being held in the Busovaca Military Prison until approximately the 8th of February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the number of prisoners that were there, and I don't know the date until which they were held, but I do know that there were prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those prisoners taken out to dig trenches on front-lines and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, although the information that I have personally received, as I worked with my colleagues, said that there were such things, but this was never ordered by the commander of the Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Brigadier, try to answer as clearly as possible. I do understand that you are trying to be cautious in your answers, but if you read the answer that I see in front of me here, "I cannot confirm that, although the indications from my colleagues said that I might be able to and that it wouldn't be the commander. I would like," -- this is a Tribunal and I am asking that you understand that. Reread the sentence, logically it is not very good.
